findings.text: The first lines tell a newcomer what Athena is in plain words: what it does, what it is written in, and how it works (one model works, another checks). This is the strongest part of the page for a first-time reader.
findings.source: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. It shows how it read the request, has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost."

findings.text: The URL is Athena's own site, but almost the whole page is about a different project, firstmate. Athena gets one sentence. A newcomer who came to learn about Athena gets little on why they would use it beyond 'it can do this', and has to work out that the page is a demonstration.
findings.source: <title>Athena explains how firstmate handles work</title>; header ledes

findings.text: The page does say why it exists. The proof is visible: every bullet has claim links, and every claim links to file lines at a fixed commit, so a sceptical reader can check it.
findings.source: "Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it with every statement traced to a claim, and every claim to lines in the project's own files."

findings.text: Next steps are easy to find, because the header links to them, and they are concrete. But the install step doesn't say what is needed first (a Rust toolchain, model access or API keys), and doesn't say where to run the command.
findings.source: Next steps: "Install Athena from a checkout of its repository: ./setup.sh" and "Try it with a one-line request: athena ask \"add a changelog\""

findings.text: The section called 'Start here' quickly gets into exit codes, locks, "unheld, unblocked" items and "guarded fast-forward". Someone new to both projects will find it dense long before they could judge whether firstmate or Athena is useful to them.
findings.source: Start here / One piece of work: "If every place of a declared capacity is held, the spawn exits 75 and the item stays queued."

findings.text: Some key terms are used but never defined. 'Open captain call' and 'merge authority' have no glossary entry. 'Stale wake' is defined using itself ("A wake after which…"), and 'heartbeat' is not explained at all.
findings.source: "If the backlog item is still an open captain call, teardown reopens it instead of closing it."

findings.text: The glossary entry for 'ship', one of the main task kinds, doesn't actually say what a ship is. The plain meaning only appears earlier, in "A ship changes a project".
findings.source: Glossary: "ship — A kind of task, named next to scouts."

findings.text: Each line in the states list is only a name, a tag and citations. The reader has to scroll to the glossary to learn what each state means.
findings.source: States of a piece of work: "queued initial"

findings.text: The page is open about what it did not check: nothing was run, and some paths were missed on the first reading. This builds trust, though it is placed after the long glossary, where a newcomer may never see it.
findings.source: Limits of this study: "This study read the pinned tree only... no failure or retry edge was observed; every claim is marked read."
